(p-210) Surat al-'Adiyat (The Chargers) — its purpose

It is to inform that most of creation will be ruined on the Day of the Quake, because they preferred the perishing glory and wealth [and property] to the enduring reward with the Lord of Majesty. This is indicated by the oath, which consists of "by the chargers" (al-'Adiyat), the thing sworn by, and the thing sworn to, and what is joined to it. It is known that its name is the most indicative thing of this, because of what the oath and the thing sworn to guide to: "In the name of Allah" (bismillah), to whom belongs all command, so He is not questioned about what He does; "the Most Gracious" (al-Rahman), who encompassed all with the blessing of His bringing into existence and His making clear, so His blessing is the most complete and comprehensive blessing; "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who singled out the sincere of His servants with His guidance, so He perfected and completed His blessing upon them.

* *

When He concluded Surat al-Zalzalah (The Earthquake) with the recompense for evil deeds on the Day of Judgement (al-Fasl, the Decisive Day), He opened this surah by explaining what leads to those deeds from natural disposition (ṭab') and what that disposition is drawn towards of benefit that it imagines. He rebukes the one who does not prepare for that Day by thorough caution against those deeds, reproaching the one who prefers his worldly life over his afterlife. He swears by what occurs only in the case of people of great blessings, which necessitate gratitude. Whoever is dominated by the spirit (al-ruh) gives thanks, and whoever is dominated by the natural disposition (al-ṭab') — and they are the majority — disbelieves. So He says: ﴿By the chargers﴾, that is, the animals whose nature is to run at the utmost speed, and they are the horses, whose backs are a source of honour and whose bellies are a treasure. They are a burden for one man and a reward for another. Whoever boasts of them and calls the people of Islam by them, and the pride of their honour makes him insolent until he cuts the road and frightens the travellers, they become an evil for him. Whoever makes them for the sake of Allah, they become a reward for him. Whoever rides them and does not forget Allah's right concerning their necks and their backs, they become a covering (sitr) for him. He swore by them only so that one would reflect upon the great secrets in them, by which they are distinguished from similar animals such as the bull, for example, and the donkey, so that he may know that the One who singled them out with this is a single, choosing Doer, the Subduer.

So the oath is, in reality, by Him, glorified is He.

And since they indicate the ones that snort (al-ḍābiḥat) by necessary implication, He said, with ﴿ḍabḥan﴾ governing it, or governing a presumed ﴿tuḍbaḥu﴾ [it is snorted]: ﴿ḍabḥan﴾ (snorting). [Al-ḍabḥ] is a loud sound from their mouths at the intense running, not a neighing (ṣahīl), nor a whinnying (ḥamḥamah), nor a roaring (rughā'), and it is the breath. None of the animals is described as snorting except the horse, the dog and the fox. Its original usage is for the fox, and it was borrowed for horses. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported it and said: "aḥḥ aḥḥ" — or ḍabḥ is running below the (fast) gallop (taqrīb).

(p-212) When He mentioned their charging (ʿadw), He followed it with what arises from it, saying, joining with the particle of consequence (fa), because the charging is such that striking fire (īrāʾ) is caused by it and follows it: ﴿By those that strike sparks﴾, that is, those that bring forth fire by what their hooves strike against the stones, especially when traversing rough terrain.

And since īrāʾ is the effect of qadaḥ (striking), He said: ﴿striking sparks﴾, that is, they are struck with violent blows like the striking of a flint (zind) so as to kindle the fire. He attributed the īrāʾ to them because they bring about its form, even though they have no intention toward it.

Since he mentioned the charging (al-'adw) and what results from it, he mentioned its outcome and its end, and so he said: ﴿Then those that raid﴾, meaning, by the raiding of their riders upon the enemy [the charging and the] raiding, and the intense galloping, for the purpose of killing and plunder. And since the raid, from which ruin and woe result, is at its most startling when it occurs at the tail end of the night, he said: ﴿at dawn﴾, meaning, those that enter upon the morning.

Since, in the course of a raid, the enemy's position keeps shifting—sometimes to the right, sometimes to the left, sometimes in front, and sometimes behind, according to the advancing and retreating in the exchange of attack and maneuver—sometimes they are pursuing one who flees, and at other times they are engaging one who advances to fight, dust arises from this in great quantity, stirring up the air for it and causing its particles to collide with one another, so that they oppose the horses with the force of their thrust from their hooves and with what those hooves stir up from it. And since the thing sworn by was considered in itself, while the result of the oath was considered in terms of the action, initially and with primary regard set aside from the essence, it was conjoined to the active participle after being resolved into a verb until it reached them, so He said: ﴿Then they raise thereby﴾ [i.e., by the act of raiding, and its place and time, from the intensity of the enemy] ﴿dust﴾, i.e., dust, together with the necks, the shouting, and the driving on with the neck, until that dust became woven and compacted over them.

Since the raider usually penetrates the midst of a company when their condition is disturbed, scattering their unity—for whenever they become separated, disorder takes hold among them, and whenever they disagree, the enemy slips in among them and so breaks up their unity—He said: ﴿So they burst into the midst thereof﴾, that is, by that dust-cloud, or by that action, the time and the place, ﴿a company﴾, that is, the very target of the raid. Thus they penetrated into the middle of that company, owing to their (the horses') courage, strength and obedience, and the courage of their riders.

When He swore by the horses, which are the noblest of animals, He was also swearing by the human being for whose sake the oath is made, since man is the noblest of what is characterized by eloquence. His thoughts run through his mind like racehorses, and meanings are struck out of it, sometimes joined to the most brilliant radiance and sometimes to the basest things that can be joined to them, namely falsehood and slander, heresy and tyranny. From it the sharpest minds are led astray: sometimes by means of proof they overturn the doubts of adversaries, and sometimes by means of what changes the ambiguous doubts into fine meanings. Sometimes it scatters sound meanings before the people of tyranny (p. 214) from among the people of innovation and disbelief, and sometimes it scatters corrupt meanings before the party of the Sovereign, the Judge. Sometimes it places itself among the company of the tyrants, and sometimes among the company of the believers.

The raid was, for the most part, carried out to subdue those raided and seize their wealth, an act of aggression if it was outside of jihad. If it was in jihad, few are sincere in that state, so that his action is for God alone, as the sacred hadith points to: "Indeed, My servant, every servant of Mine, is the one who remembers Me at the meeting of his opponent." Here He answers the oath by mentioning what the oath is made about, judging the human species, on the basis that counting the sincere is, because of their scarcity, as nothing. He confirms what they have of denying this, for everyone disowns such a state: ﴿Indeed, man﴾, that is, this species, with its attachment to itself and its forgetfulness of what benefits it, ﴿is ungrateful to his Lord﴾, that is, to the One who has done good to him by originating him, then sustaining him, managing him and nurturing him, ﴿and indeed he is a kanud﴾. Kanud (كَنُود) means one who is ungrateful and wretched because of his bad conduct, in that he gives precedence, over what God has bestowed on him of the swift noble horses and of the strength of heart and limbs, to what He has forbidden him. Its verbal noun is al-kanud, with a damma, which is kufran al-ni'mah (ingratitude for blessing). So what is meant here by expressing it in this form, which is for emphasis, is one who belittles the little and does not thank for the much, who forgets the abundance of blessing because of a small trial, and who blames his Lord for the slightest affliction. Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: it is the one whom a single characteristic of wrongdoing has made forget many characteristics of goodness. Its opposite is the shakur (the very grateful).

The Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: He, glorified is He, swore concerning the state of man by what he is, saying: ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord﴾, that is, a disbeliever, who is stingy with what he has of wealth, as though he will not be recompensed or called to account for little or much of it, from where he acquired it and on what he spent it. It is as though he had not heard His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7] ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 8]. ﴿And indeed he is, in his love of wealth, intense﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8], that is, of wealth, ﴿intensely﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8], that is, stingy.

﴿And indeed he is, of that, a witness﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 7], for God is, concerning that, fully aware, so there is no concern for his affair and the outcome of his end. ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 9] ﴿and what is in the breasts is made apparent﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 10], that is, what is in them of good and evil is distinguished, so that the recompense may fall upon it. ﴿Indeed, their Lord, that Day, is fully Aware of them﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 11], nothing of their affairs being hidden from Him. ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7] ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 8]. — End.

Since a human being's proceeding into wrongdoing is a wonder, and if he bears witness against himself to wrongdoing it is even more wondrous, He said, emphasizing what most of creation denies before the Resurrection and the (divine) cross-examination of their ingratitude: ﴿And indeed he﴾, that is, the human being, ﴿is, concerning that﴾, that is, the great ingrate, in that he proceeded to oppose the greatest King, the Benefactor, along with disbelief in His favor (p-216) ﴿a witness﴾, because when he is cross-examined he acknowledges that everything he has is from his Lord's benevolence, and that his Lord forbade him from disobedience; or [he acknowledges] that there is no excuse [from Him] for what he did, and that it is not befitting for any intelligent person to make a movement that the king he serves might dislike, when he has nothing except from him and without his permission; and that if he moves otherwise, he is a disbeliever in his benefactor, deserving of his punishment, and cannot deny any part of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 100, verse 8:

Since it is among the wonders that a person should deny the favour of the Benefactor while he himself is a witness against himself, he mentioned what drives him to that, so that it becomes trivial to him, and said: ﴿And indeed he﴾, i.e., man, insofar as he is such, together with his own testimony against himself of disbelief, which requires the removal of blessings, ﴿is, in his love﴾, i.e., because of his love of ﴿the good﴾, i.e., wealth, which, owing to his ignorance, he counts as nothing other than good, ﴿intense﴾, i.e., stingy with wealth, restricting it and holding on to it, or intense in strength in his love, because its benefit is in this world, and he is bound to the immediate, present, and sensible, while knowing that the least of what is in it is that it preoccupies him from fine service to his Lord, while he turns away from the religion, since its benefit is deferred and absent. Along with his knowledge that the one who has been made aware of what pleases his Lord in service, who urges it and calls to it, is, for the love of worshipping God, weak and sluggish. His love of good should have required gratitude from him, which demands increase. It should not be imagined that ﴿intense﴾ governs ﴿love﴾, because what follows the lam does not govern what precedes it; rather, that preceding word is evidence for an omitted object that is governed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 100, verse 9:

(p-217) Since wealth is perishable, it is not fitting for a person of intellect to hang his hope on it, let alone prefer it over what endures, so He alerted him to this with an eloquent warning, saying, as a consequence of this and in a tone of wonder, placing him in a position where he must face what his affair will lead to: ﴿Does he not know﴾, i.e., this human being whom his worldly comfort has made heedless of himself.

Since love is an inner matter, which none knows except the One who knows the unseen, and since resurrection is from the realm of the unseen, and is a matter that is unavoidable, and since the one who causes fear is unspecified in his existence, there was no need to specify the agent. So He used the passive form in His saying, threatening and indicating that He is utterly capable of stirring up what is hidden, linking to what He will decree the outcome of his affair: that Allah will call him to account and recompense him for his deeds, and that neither wealth nor anything else will benefit him, and nothing will save him except those of his deeds that conformed to the command of his Lord, were built on the foundation of faith, and were done sincerely: ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾, i.e., is stirred up with the greatest ease, brought out, separated, examined and searched with the greatest ease.

Since the dead are inanimate before resurrection, He expressed it with the particle used for that which does not reason, saying: ﴿what is in the graves﴾, i.e., brings out those within them of the dead, whom the Arabs denied would be raised, so that they are gathered for the reckoning; or [brings out] from their bones, flesh, sinews, skins and all their bodies, and turns some of it over onto other parts until every part of it is restored to what it was, then the spirit is returned to it, so that each person is as he died.

Since what is feared is only what follows from the resurrection, namely the recompense for corrupt deeds, He said: ﴿And what is in the breasts is brought forth﴾, i.e., extracted, distinguished and gathered, so that it is known that all of it is recorded with the utmost ease, as the passive construction indicates; ﴿what is in the breasts﴾, i.e., whether good or evil, of that which the one who harbors it thinks no one knows at all. It appears written in the books of deeds. This indicates that intentions (niyyat) are called to account just as what appears of their effects is called to account.

When the knowledge of what is in the breasts was a striking matter for the intellect, He said, combining the sense (al-ma'na) in contrast to what He expressed with the singular, with regard to the wording (al-lafz): because knowledge of the whole entails knowledge of the part, but not the reverse. He emphasized it as a sign that it is something that is hardly believed. He gave the reason for the omitted clause that indicates the reckoning: ﴿Indeed, their Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to them by creating them, providing for them, nurturing them, and making them strong and sound. ﴿with them﴾. He placed this prepositional phrase first not for exclusivity (al-ikhtisas), but to indicate the ultimate point of the statement.

Since awareness (al-khibra) means encompassing a thing outwardly and inwardly, and since it follows that awareness of a thing after it has happened is, by a greater degree, awareness of it while it is happening, He said: ﴿on that Day﴾, that is, when these matters occur, which is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿surely is All-Aware﴾, that is, encompassing them from all directions, knowing to the utmost degree the inner states of their affairs. How, then, would He not know their outward affairs, both substances and accidents, words and deeds, whether hidden or manifest, secret or open, good or evil? It is known that among them there is injustice and other things, and among them there is the doer of good and others. Because of His, glory be to Him, complete knowledge of all this, He calls them to account, lest what contradicts wisdom occur, namely that good and evil be made equal. Thus the purpose of the restriction and the fronting of the adverbial phrase is to convey emphasis in the description that He, glory be to Him and exalted, has comprehensive knowledge of all this, just as when it is said to you: "Do you know so-and-so?" and you reply: "I know none but Him." Your intention is that your knowledge of him is of the utmost precision, not a denial of others' knowledge of him. This also implies that every person, on that Day, will understand with the utmost clarity that He, glory be to Him and exalted, is [knowing] of their states, and that He is never heedless of any of it, unlike what happens in this world, where a person does many things while being unmindful that his Lord, glory be to Him, is observing him in them, even if he were reminded of this knowledge. Because of His, glory be to Him and exalted, encompassing all their states, He was knowing that man is, towards his Lord, ungrateful (﴿kanūd﴾). Its last part has returned to its first, and its detailed part has taken on the explanation of its summary. And God is the Guide to what is right.
